flashcards.front: How many keys move on average when adding 1 node to a N-node Consistent Hashing ring?
flashcards.back: Only ~K/N keys move (only keys falling in the new node's clockwise arcs), compared to ~(N-1)/N keys under naive modulo hashing `hash(key) % N`.

flashcards.front: Why do production hash rings assign 150–200 virtual nodes (vnodes) per physical server?
flashcards.back: With few physical nodes, random hash positions cause severe imbalance; interleaving hundreds of vnodes reduces variance to ~5% and spreads orphaned load evenly across all surviving servers when one node fails.

quizzes.scenario: You grow a 10-node Memcached fleet to 11 nodes using server = hash(key) % N instead of consistent hashing.
quizzes.question: Roughly what fraction of keys now map to a different server?
options: None of the keys, as existing entries stay where they are
About 91% of keys, close to 10 out of every 11
About 9% of keys, the share owned by the new node
About 50% of keys, since half the remainders shift
quizzes.explanation: Changing the modulus from 10 to 11 changes hash(key) % N for about 10 of every 11 keys, so roughly 91% of keys miss at once. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/11 of the keys.
optionExplanations: Entries stay on the old servers, but lookups now go to new ones and miss.
Correct. Almost every key's remainder changes when N changes.
That is the consistent-hashing result; plain modulo reshuffles far more.
There is no reason for half; the remainder changes for most keys.

quizzes.scenario: Your ring has 200 virtual nodes per shard, yet shard 4 is at 100% CPU because one celebrity profile accounts for 35% of all reads.
quizzes.question: Do more virtual nodes fix this, and if not, what does?
options: No; only moving to range partitioning removes the hotspot
Yes; more vnodes split each key's reads across shards
Yes; switching to a better hash function evens the load
No; cache the key locally or spread copies with salted keys
quizzes.explanation: Virtual nodes balance how many keys each shard owns, not how hot a single key is. One key still hashes to one position. Hot keys need a local in-process cache, read replicas for that key, or salting the key into several copies.
optionExplanations: Range partitioning still puts one key on one shard, so the hotspot remains.
Vnodes split the key space, but a single key still maps to one shard.
A better hash spreads many keys evenly; it cannot split one key.
Correct. A single key always lands on one ring position.
